title: Short Stuff: Why Does Time Speed Up As You Age?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore why time seems to speed up as people age. They cover a 1990s study by psychologist Peter Mangan in which young and older participants estimated three minutes by counting, with older subjects running short. They discuss the theory of a slowing internal brain clock (tied to heartbeat, breathing, metabolism, and a midbrain location), the role of novelty and new experiences versus routine (including Steve Taylor's book Making Time), dopamine decline with age, and the logarithmic-scale idea championed by Christian Yates of the University of Bath, where each year is a shrinking proportion of a lifetime. The episode closes with a lighthearted take-away about gratitude and living fully.
topics: why time speeds up as you age
heartbeat and breathing and time perception

segments.title: New Year opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the new year with light banter about future food pills and the feeling that time is flying, setting up the question of why it speeds up.

segments.title: Peter Mangan counting experiment
segments.summary: Josh describes the 1990s study by psychologist Peter Mangan, in which young people and older adults counted out three minutes. The younger group averaged close to three minutes, while the older group averaged about 3:40, suggesting their internal clock runs slowly.

segments.title: Internal clock slowing with heartbeat and metabolism
segments.summary: The hosts explain that metabolism, breathing and heartbeat slow with age, and that the brain's internal timing clock may use these bodily cues. Faster kid heartbeats make time seem slower to children, and slowing rates in adults make time seem to speed up. The clock is theoretical and thought to sit in the midbrain.
topics: heartbeat and breathing and time perception

segments.title: Novelty, routine and new experiences
segments.summary: Children have many new experiences, while adult routines are repetitive, so the brain processes less novel information and time seems to pass faster. The hosts muse about testing this by having adults experience only new things. They also contrast childhood and adult perceptions of car trips to vacations.

segments.title: Steve Taylor and familiarity
segments.summary: Steve Taylor, author of Making Time, argues that familiar experiences barely register, so time seems to pass more quickly as we process less new information.

segments.title: Dopamine decline with age
segments.summary: The hosts note that dopamine hits decline with age, possibly because novel stimuli come less often, and that dopamine may help train the midbrain clock, so lower dopamine may be part of the clock slowing.

segments.title: Logarithmic scale of a lifetime
segments.summary: Josh explains logarithmic versus linear scales using the Richter scale, then applies the idea to life: one year is a shrinking fraction of life as you age. Christian Yates of the University of Bath is cited on why summers and birthdays seem to take longer when young and zip by later.

segments.title: Closing thoughts and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about feeling depressed, then conclude they should take the idea as motivation to appreciate the year and live fully. The episode ends with the standard sign-off.
